description: Taniwha are supernatural beings of Māori tradition who dwell in rivers, lakes, deep pools, and the sea, guarding tribal waterways and landmarks. Some, like Ngake and Whātaitai, are protective kaitiaki linked to hapū and iwi; others are feared man-eaters who seize travellers. They may appear as giant lizards, sharks, whales, or serpents, their presence marking dangerous waters.
research_notes: Verified via Te Ara and Wikipedia (Taniwha). Folds in input's protective-guardian vs man-eating duality and the Ngake/Whātaitai example.

description: Taotaomo'na, the 'people of before,' are the ancestral spirits of the ancient Chamorro, told across Guam and the Northern Marianas. Said to be the ghosts of early inhabitants, they inhabit banyan trees, deep jungle, and caves, and can be hostile to those who trespass or disturb ancient sites and bones. Their displeasure is feared, and respect and proper ritual are believed to appease them.
research_notes: Verified via Wikipedia (Taotaomo'na) and Chamorro oral tradition. Description folds in input's forest/cave habitat and guardian behavior.

description: Te Ngaru ('The Wave') is a culture hero of Mangaia in the Cook Islands, whose exploits explain the ocean's power. Grandson of Moko the Great Lizard, he matched himself against the great ocean swell Tikokura and the man-eating shark Tumutearetoka, riding the crests of the sea in a struggle recorded by the missionary William Wyatt Gill and studied in modern scholarship.
source: Journal of the Polynesian Society (W. W. Gill, Mangaia); Michael Reilly, Cook Islands hero traditions
research_notes: Attested in the Journal of the Polynesian Society material on Mangaia (W. W. Gill) and Michael Reilly's scholarship; 'ngaru' = wave. Record reframed from generic sea-spirit to the documented culture hero.

description: Tiddalik is a giant frog of Gunaikurnai (south-eastern Australian) Dreaming tradition who drank all the water of the world, leaving the land dry and thirsty. To break his spell, the other animals made him laugh; when he did, the waters burst from him to fill the rivers, lakes, and billabongs. His story is told as the origin of the continent's waters.
research_notes: Verified via Wikipedia (Tiddalik); Gunaikurnai origin. Folds in input's drought-relief narrative.

description: Tui Fiti ('Lord of Fiji') is the eel god of Polynesian legend, best known from the Samoan story of Sina and the Eel: a Fijian lord who, transformed into an eel, is beheaded by Sina and buried, and from whose head grows the first coconut tree. The name is also a Fijian chiefly title. The tale explains the coconut and the origins of a chiefly line.
source: Samoan oral tradition (Sina and the Eel); Polynesian mythology
research_notes: Verified via the Samoan 'Sina and the Eel' legend (Tui Fiti as eel god) and the Fijian chiefly title. Description corrects the input's 'god of war at hill temples' framing to the documented coconut-origin tale.

description: Tāne Mahuta is the Māori god of forests and birds, the son of Ranginui (Sky Father) and Papatūānuku (Earth Mother) who forced the two apart to let light into the world. He clothed his mother's body with trees and creatures, fathered the birds and insects, and created the first woman Hineahuone. The famous kauri tree Tāne Mahuta in Waipoua Forest bears his name.
research_notes: Verified via Wikipedia (Tāne Mahuta) and Te Ara (Tāne). Folds in input's forest/bird guardianship and the famous kauri.

description: Tāwhaki is a semi-divine hero and atua of lightning and thunder in Māori tradition, a grandson of the sky who slew the man-eating bird-ogre Matuku-tangotango, freed his kinswoman Whaitiri from its belly, and climbed to the heavens, returning with the powers of lightning and thunder. He is closely linked to sacred mountains, and he is said to appear to heroes in disguise to test their worth.
research_notes: Verified via Wikipedia (Tāwhaki); folds in the Matuku-tangotango episode, the thunder connection, and the disguise-testing motif from the input.

description: Te Pusi mo te Ali ('The Eel and the Flounder') is a Tuvaluan creation tale of the lagoon: an eel and a flatfish are bound in a conflict or agreement that shapes the lagoon's life, and eels are regarded as sacred and tapu in Tuvaluan tradition. The story carries the lagoon-based world-view of the atolls.
research_notes: Attested as Tuvaluan lagoon creation story (the eel and the flounder) per input and Tuvaluan oral tradition; eels are sacred/tapu. Some narrative detail uncertain — kept general, quality fair.

description: Tefolaha is the founding ancestor of Nanumea atoll in Tuvalu, a partly divine hero said to have come from Tonga and to have established the island's chiefly lines. His spear Kaumaile is a treasured heirloom of the island, and descent from him is claimed by Nanumea's principal families, making him a central figure of Tuvaluan island-origin traditions.
research_notes: Verified via Wikipedia (Tuvaluan mythology): Nanumea's founding ancestor from Tonga, half-man half-spirit, spear Kaumaile. Folds in input's island-builder framing.

description: Telematua is a legendary giant-ancestor of Tuvaluan tradition, a being of colossal size said to have shaped the islands and their channels; his passage or labour is recalled as the origin of the passages (ava) between islets. Sluggish and indifferent to humans in most accounts, he is nonetheless a figure of the islands' ancient founding stories.
research_notes: Giant-ancestor figure of Tuvaluan tradition per input and regional accounts; exact island attribution varies (Funafuti/Vaitupu tellings). Kept general; quality fair.

description: Tepuhi is the founding ancestor of Nanumaga atoll in Tuvalu, a spirit who is said to have come from Fiji in the form of a sea serpent and to have established the island's people. Unlike Nanumea's ancestor Tefolaha, who came from Tonga as a half-human hero, Tepuhi's serpent form ties Nanumaga's origin to the ocean and to the spirit world.
research_notes: Verified via Wikipedia (Tuvaluan mythology): Nanumaga's founding ancestor, sea-serpent form, came from Fiji; contrasted with Tefolaha of Nanumea.

description: Ma'i is the Samoan spirit of sickness and epidemic: in traditional belief, illness is often inflicted by aitu spirits or by sorcery, and the ma'i is the disease-spirit itself. Such afflictions are understood to punish social or ritual transgression and to be relieved through appeasement, ritual, and the intervention of specialists, linking health to moral and spiritual order.

research_notes: Attested in Samoan ethnographic literature on spirit-caused illness (Lazar, Mageo, Goodman). Description aligns the disease-spirit framing with documented aitu/sorcery beliefs.

description: Matuku-tangotango is the giant man-eating bird of Māori tradition, a monstrous owl-like creature who swallowed the ancestress Whaitiri and devoured travellers. The hero Tāwhaki slew him and cut open his belly to free his relatives. The name matuku also denotes the bittern, and the ogre's image blends the fearsome night-bird with the taniwha-like predators of old.
research_notes: Verified via Wikipedia (Matuku-tangotango); description folds in the Tāwhaki-cycle episode and the bittern word-sense.

description: In Hawaiian tradition, Māui is the trickster demigod and culture hero who fished up the islands with his enchanted fishhook (the constellation Māui's Fishhook), snared the sun to lengthen the day, and drew fire from the depths. The youngest and cleverest of brothers, he used cunning rather than strength to aid humanity, and his exploits explain the shape of land and sky.
research_notes: Verified via Wikipedia (Māui) for the Hawaiian tradition (island-fishing, sun-snaring, fire). Folds in input's trickster framing.

description: In Māori tradition, Māui is the great demigod and trickster who fished up Te Ika-a-Māui, the North Island, from the sea with a hook made from the jawbone of his grandmother Murirangawhenua, his canoe becoming Te Waka a Māui, the South Island. He slowed the sun, stole fire from Mahuika, and sought immortality from Hine-nui-te-pō, shaping the human condition.
research_notes: Verified via Te Ara and Wikipedia for the Māori feats (Te Ika-a-Māui, Te Waka a Māui, sun, fire). Folds in input.

description: The Menehune are the legendary dwarf builders of Hawaiʻi, said to have raised temples (heiau), fishponds, roads, and canoes in a single night, working only in darkness and vanishing at dawn if unfinished. The 1820 census of Kauaʻi listed 65 of them. Scholars debate whether they remember earlier settlers (manahune, 'commoners') or are a post-contact invention, but their craftwork lore endures.
research_notes: Verified via Wikipedia (Menehune) incl. 1820 Kauaʻi census, night-work, and the manahune/Luomala debate. Folds in input.

description: The Mimi (Mimih) are tall, extremely thin spirit beings of Arnhem Land and Kakadu who live in the rock crevices and escarpments and are so delicate that a strong wind can break them. They are credited with making the first rock paintings, and with teaching Aboriginal people painting, hunting, and cooking. Usually shy, they can be dangerous if their places or pets are disturbed.
research_notes: Verified via Wikipedia (Mimih/Mimi) and IDAIA on Maningrida traditions (Kunwok, Rembarrnga, Dalabon, Djawoyn). Folds in input's rich appearance/behavior fields.

In Aboriginal accounts such beings enforce cultural law and warn children not to wander; in modern folklore it is also a Bigfoot-like cryptid.
